messages.subject: Enserco — exposure run review, Apr 17–19
messages.body:
Following up on the limit-breach question you raised this morning.

Pulled the daily exposure workbooks Tana runs for Enserco. The Apr 17 close shows $4.2M net of L/C collateral — clean, inside the $5M ceiling. The Apr 18 close is $5.3M net. That's the crossing point; the limit was gone by end of day Apr 18.

What the workbook entry says for Apr 18 is 'approaching limit / collateral review pending.' That language doesn't reflect what the number actually shows.

More to the point: the ticket log for Apr 18 afternoon and Apr 19 shows at least three trades booked after the $5.3M figure was on the screen. Tana processed that batch — her initials are on the clearance queue for each one. So the trades that pushed through after the line crossed weren't a system gap; they went through the normal workflow.

I'd want to know when the over-limit alert was supposed to go out and why it didn't, but that's a separate thread. For now the exposure picture is: counterparty is over its approved ceiling, has been since Apr 18 close, and additional volume was booked on top of that.

Let me know how you want to handle escalation.

Sara —

Following up on the demand letter I drafted and sent to Elizabeth in early April. Elizabeth held it pending the commercial round; I flagged at the time that the 90-day trigger off the settlement date was running. That window closed April 28. No demand was filed before cutoff.

I've checked the master agreement language twice. The trigger is hard — 90 days from settlement, no tolling provision, no cure period. We're past it. The right to compel arbitration against the counterparty under that agreement is gone.

Elizabeth has the full file. I wanted to make sure you had visibility given where the negotiations appear to be heading.

— Tana

messages.subject: Re: counterparty Online Agreement — point #6 arbitration language
messages.body:
Richard —

I've reviewed the counterparty's proposed arbitration language at point #6. The restriction to monetary damages only, with specific performance carved out, is a significant concession for us to make, and I would not recommend accepting it as drafted. Our arbitration right under the master agreement is intact and gives us meaningful leverage here. I'd push back and insist on preserving the full remedial menu — including specific performance — before we agree to any revised Online Agreement language. We are in a strong procedural posture to do so. Let me know if you want me to draft the counter-language.

— Elizabeth

messages.subject: Re: counterparty Online Agreement — point #6 arbitration language
messages.body:
Elizabeth —

Thanks — that's the read I needed. On the strength of your confirmation that the arbitration right is intact and that we're in a strong procedural posture, I'm going ahead with a firm response to the counterparty's negotiating team today. I'm directing them through Carol and Sara that we cannot accept the limitation to monetary damages only, that Enron reserves its full arbitration rights under the master agreement including the right to seek specific performance, and that if they insist on the carve-out we are prepared to invoke those rights formally rather than continue negotiating on their terms.

I want the counterparty to understand this is not a placeholder position — we are treating arbitration as a live option and the letter will say so plainly. Please do draft counter-language for point #6 so we have something concrete to put in front of them if they push back.

— Richard

answer.concealment: A contract attorney conceals from the trading desk that the price index or benchmark rate specified in a master agreement has already been formally declared inapplicable or discontinued by the relevant publishing body, allowing the desk to continue pricing and settling trades as though that index is still the valid contractual reference, because admitting the discontinuation would force an immediate renegotiation of the fallback rate and expose that the attorney had received the notice and failed to flag it.
answer.actor: Mark Taylor — the concealer, legal and regulatory information hub who received and suppressed the discontinuation notice
answer.victim: Sara Shackleton — the misled party, legal and regulatory coordinator who relies on Mark Taylor's representations to direct the trading desk's pricing work
answer.true_fact: The publishing body that maintains the Enron Canadian Daily Index specified in the master agreement has formally declared that index discontinued and inapplicable as a contractual reference, effective immediately; Mark Taylor received the written notice from the publishing body several days before the events below.
answer.false_belief: Sara Shackleton, and through her the trading desk, believes the Enron Canadian Daily Index is still a fully valid, operative contractual reference rate and that the only open questions about it are the holiday-language drafting issue and the CFTC regulatory question Mark Taylor has already flagged — both of which are framed as routine, solvable problems, not existential ones.

atoms.fact: The benchmark index named in the master agreement has been formally declared discontinued and is no longer a valid contractual reference by the body that publishes it.
Mark Taylor received the written discontinuation notice from the publishing body and saved it to a subfolder before the events described.
Mark Taylor told Sara Shackleton that the index reference in the master agreement was correct and operative and that she saw no issue with it.
Sara Shackleton directed the trading desk to treat the index as the valid settlement reference and begin preparing trade confirmations on the basis of Mark Taylor's assurance.

messages.subject: Re: Canadian index transition — follow-up from publishing body
messages.body:
Picking up from our call — wanted to get this in writing before end of day.

The Canadian energy price-reporting body sent formal written notice on 2/11 declaring the Enron Daily Index discontinued effective March 1. The notice is unambiguous: the series is no longer a valid contractual reference for settlement or pricing purposes under any agreement that cites it by name. They're instructing all counterparties to transition to the successor methodology or negotiate fallback language before pricing any further trades against the old series.

I flagged this to you because the series is the one named in Enron's Canadian trading master agreements — so anyone relying on it for settlement right now is on thin ice contractually.

On distribution: the 2/11 notice went to the legal owner of the master agreement language, which is Mark. She would have received it directly. If she hasn't surfaced it yet I'd want to know why, because the transition deadline is real and the desk needs to know.

Let me know if you want me to loop in compliance or if you'd rather take it up the chain first.

messages.subject: Re: Canadian platform — index question before afternoon call
messages.body:
The index reference is fine — that's not one of our open items.

The two issues I flagged to Greg are the only ones: the holiday-language redundancy, which is a clean drafting fix, and the CFTC scrutiny question on price discovery, which I expect to resolve this afternoon once I hear back from CFTC counsel. On the index itself, we're good. The Enron Daily Index is the correct and operative reference under the master agreement and I see no issue there.

Once we get the CFTC answer we should be in a position to tell the desk to proceed.

— Mark

messages.subject: Re: Canadian platform — index question before afternoon call
messages.body:
Per Mark, the index reference is confirmed good. The open items are the holiday language and the CFTC question, both in progress.

Please let the trading desk know they can treat the Enron Daily Index as the valid settlement reference and begin preparing the first trade confirmations accordingly. I'm directing the desk to proceed on that basis — no hold on the index, no unwind required. We'll send a final green light once the CFTC answer comes in, but the index itself is not a blocker.

— Sara
